title: Displacement of two native crayfishes, Cambarus howardi Hobbs & Hall, 1969 and Cambarus latimanus (Le Conte, 1856), from preferred thermal zones by the non-indigenous Procambarus clarkii (Girard, 1852) (Decapoda: Astacidea: Cambaridae)
content:
Abstract
Urbanization and climate change are increasing stream temperatures, potentially altering aquatic community structure through physiological stress and enhanced competition for thermal refuges. Crayfishes, as ectothermic ecosystem engineers, are especially vulnerable to warming and invasive species pressures. We established thermal zone preferences of two native South Carolina crayfishes, Cambarus howardi Hobbs & Hall, 1969 and Cambarus latimanus (Le Conte, 1856), and one non-native species, Procambarus clarkii (Girard, 1852) under laboratory conditions and then assessed whether the presence of P. clarkii displaced native species from preferred thermal habitats. Individuals of each species were observed in thermal gradient arenas to determine temperature preferences. Both C. howardi (P = 0.003) and C. latimanus (P < 0.001) exhibited a significant preference for cooler zones, whereas P. clarkii showed no thermal preference (P = 0.66). Resident-intruder trials were tested whether P. clarkii could displace natives from preferred zones. Whereas C. howardi had no significant shift in thermal zone use (χ² = 1.68, P = 0.431), C. latimanus significantly altered (χ² = 16.99, P < 0.001) its thermal zone use in the presence of P. clarkii, indicating behavioral displacement. Logistic regression revealed that displacement probability increased with intruder body size (P = 0.046), with the largest-size species (P. clarkii) frequently excluding native crayfish from cooler refuges. These findings suggest that warming-induced competition for thermal refuges may amplify the ecological impact of invasive crayfishes. Protecting cold-water microhabitats and mitigating species introductions may be critical for conserving native crayfish diversity in thermally vulnerable ecosystems.
